explanations.explanation: That's the word, baker. Paul says, "…you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness." Notice he doesn't say to hand the person a lecture and a clipboard. Restoring means helping him back up, and Paul points the spiritual ones toward that (Galatians 6:1).

I get it, friend. Some folks hear "caught" and their thumbs go straight to the group chat. But Paul says nothing about reporting. He says the spiritual ones "should restore him with a spirit of gentleness" (Galatians 6:1). The goal is getting him back on his feet.

Crossing the street and pretending you're busy looking at your phone? Not Paul's plan. He says, "…you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness" (Galatians 6:1). You can't restore somebody from across the street, baker.

Yes, baker! Paul says to restore him "with a spirit of gentleness" (Galatians 6:1). Gentleness is how it's done. Think of how you'd handle a fresh batch of cookies straight out of the oven: slow hands and no slamming.

This one's true, friend. Paul really does say the restoring should be done "with a spirit of gentleness" (Galatians 6:1). He doesn't say with a loud voice or a pointed finger. Gentle is the way he wants it.

That's it, baker. Paul says, "But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted" (Galatians 6:1). The one doing the helping isn't above the very thing he's helping with. I'll admit that keeps me humble, because I'm the guy who needs a reminder every time.

Close to how people feel sometimes, friend, but that's not the word Paul uses. He says, "But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted" (Galatians 6:1). His worry is for the helper, that he could end up facing the same temptation.

Shunned is a heavy word, baker, and Paul doesn't use it here. He says, "But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted" (Galatians 6:1). The warning is about temptation reaching the one who's helping.

You got it, baker! Paul says, "Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). Carrying each other's weight isn't extra credit. Paul ties it right to Christ's own law.

Good guess, friend, since Moses, Israel's leader who brought the law from God, is who many people think of first. But Paul names a different one: "Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). So the answer is Christ's law.

Nope, friend, Paul doesn't mention any temple law here. He says, "Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). It's Christ's law that gets fulfilled when we carry each other's burdens.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (Galatians 6:3). Nobody else even had to be fooled. He did the whole job on his own, like a guy who talks himself into a sale and then buys it.

Reasonable, friend, since you'd think a big talker is trying to impress the crowd. But Paul says, "If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (Galatians 6:3). The one who gets fooled is the one doing the thinking.
Paul doesn't bring a teacher into this one, baker. He says, "If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (Galatians 6:3). Nobody has to be fooled but the guy himself.

Close, friend, but it's the other way around. Paul says, "Each one should test his own work. Then he will have reason to boast in himself alone, and not in someone else" (Galatians 6:4). The test shows him his own work, so there's no borrowing anybody else's.

That's right, baker! Paul says the one who tests his own work "will have reason to boast in himself alone, and not in someone else" (Galatians 6:4). So no riding on a neighbor's batch. Your own work has to stand up on its own.

Yes, baker! Paul says, "For each one should carry his own load" (Galatians 6:5). Two thoughts sit side by side here, carrying each other's burdens and carrying your own load. Paul keeps both in the same breath.
A lamp would be handy in the dark, friend, and I know that for a fact. But Paul says, "For each one should carry his own load" (Galatians 6:5). A load, not a lamp.
A staff is something a person might lean on, baker, but it's not in this verse. Paul says, "For each one should carry his own load" (Galatians 6:5). Load is the word.

That's the one, baker. Paul says the one who receives instruction "must share in all good things with his instructor" (Galatians 6:6). Notice he says all good things. He doesn't say a few crumbs off the edge of the tray.

Sounds official, friend, but Paul doesn't name a percentage here. He says the student "must share in all good things with his instructor" (Galatians 6:6). The wording is wide open, and he just says all good things.
Half the land? Whoa, friend, that'd be a big ask, and Paul doesn't ask it. He says the student "must share in all good things with his instructor" (Galatians 6:6). No acres are mentioned.
Right on, baker! Paul says, "Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return" (Galatians 6:7). Sowing comes first and reaping comes after. You get back what you planted.
Talk is cheap, friend, and I've talked plenty myself. But Paul says, "Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return" (Galatians 6:7). The word is sows, so it's about what you plant.
Hiding something is a fun idea, baker, but Paul isn't talking about that. He says, "Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return" (Galatians 6:7). What you sow is what comes back around.
That's right, baker! Paul says, "…the one who sows to please the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap eternal life" (Galatians 6:8). The Spirit is the source of that harvest.

I'd love a vault of riches too, friend, but that's not what Paul says. He says, "…the one who sows to please the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap eternal life" (Galatians 6:8). The harvest he names is eternal life.
Honor sounds nice, baker, but Paul doesn't promise it here. He says, "…the one who sows to please the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap eternal life" (Galatians 6:8). Eternal life is the harvest.

Yes, baker. Paul says, "The one who sows to please his flesh, from the flesh will reap destruction" (Galatians 6:8). It's a serious line, and Paul sets it right beside the promise about the Spirit. Both ways of sowing get their own harvest.

This one's true, friend. Paul says, "The one who sows to please his flesh, from the flesh will reap destruction" (Galatians 6:8). It's a heavy line, and he puts it right next to the promise of eternal life for the one who sows to please the Spirit.

Right, baker! Paul says, "Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up" (Galatians 6:9). The harvest comes in due time, so keep going. Even a good farmer doesn't dig up the seeds every morning to check on them.
Feast is a fun guess, friend, since I do a lot of baking for one. But Paul says, "…in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up" (Galatians 6:9). Harvest is the word he picks.
A crown sounds shiny, baker, but it's not in this verse. Paul says, "…in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up" (Galatians 6:9). He keeps with the farming picture.
Not quite, friend. Paul says, "…in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up" (Galatians 6:9). The harvest comes with not giving up, so quitting isn't part of the deal.
Right, baker! Paul says, "…in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up" (Galatians 6:9). The "if" matters there. Keep at it and don't give up.

You got it, baker! Paul says, "…let us do good to everyone, and especially to the family of faith" (Galatians 6:10). Good to everyone, with special care for the family of faith. I'm a stamper with six cookie cutter kids, so I know how family feels.

That's a kind guess, friend, and doing good surely reaches them too. But the verse names someone else. Paul says, "…let us do good to everyone, and especially to the family of faith" (Galatians 6:10).

Neighbors are a fine place to start, baker, but Paul doesn't name them here. He says, "…let us do good to everyone, and especially to the family of faith" (Galatians 6:10). The family of faith gets the special mention.
